summary: Specifies a framework for configuring SIP user agents, delivering the profile data they need to work with minimal user or administrator effort. It describes how they discover sources and request profiles.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone needs a settings file. This explains how a phone can locate where its settings are kept and download them with no fuss.

questions: what is sip ua profile delivery
what is the ua-profile event package
how does a sip phone get its configuration
what is a profile delivery server
subtitle: How a SIP phone finds its settings, downloads them and hears about changes, with no manual setup.

tldr.problem: SIP user agents need configuration data about the local network, the device and the user, and many large deployments cannot rely on pre-configuration. Vendors needed one standard way to deliver it.
tldr.mechanism: A device sends a SIP SUBSCRIBE for the new ua-profile event package, naming a profile type (local-network, device or user). The Profile Delivery Server answers with a NOTIFY that carries the profile or points to it, to be fetched over HTTP or HTTPS, and later NOTIFYs announce changes.
tldr.outcome: Devices get profiles with minimal or no user or administrator effort. The RFC does not define the profile contents, which are left to later standards.

today: RFC 6080 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2011, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the framework only; the profile contents are left to other documents.

sections.title: The Configuration Problem
sections.content:
SIP user agents need configuration data to work, such as information specific to the local network, the device and the user. A data set specific to one entity is a profile, and giving a device its profiles is profile delivery. Ideally this is automatic. Many deployments need dynamic configuration and cannot rely on pre-configuration, so RFC 6080 gives a standard method that simplifies deployments with user agents from multiple vendors. It also covers change notification when a profile changes.

The scope is limited on purpose: the framework does not define the content or format of any profile. That is left to future standardization. It also fits more than desk phones. Devices can be SIP phones or soft clients, gateways, media servers or other network elements.
sections.plainLanguage: Phones from many makers all need settings. This gives them one common way to get those settings, but it does not say what the settings contain.

sections.title: Profiles and the Delivery Server
sections.content:
Three profile types separate configuration that different parties may manage. The local-network profile comes from the local network provider and describes the network the device is connected to. The device profile comes from the device provider. The user profile comes from the SIP service provider and reflects a user's preferences and subscribed services. In a simple enterprise one provider does all three. In a complex case such as an airport kiosk on public WiFi, three different providers may each supply one.

The source of a profile is the Profile Delivery Server (PDS), made of two logical parts: the Profile Notification Component (PNC), which enrolls devices and sends notifications, and the Profile Content Component (PCC), which stores and serves profile content. The framework also defines three stages: enrollment, content retrieval and change notification.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three settings sheets: one from the building you are in, one from the maker of the phone, and one from your own phone company. A server hands them out.

sections.title: Enrollment, Retrieval and Change Notification
sections.content:
Enrollment starts when the device sends a SIP SUBSCRIBE for the ua-profile event package, using the profile-type parameter to say which profile it wants. Each profile type needs its own enrollment request. Devices and PDSs MUST implement all three types, and by default a device enrolls in this order: local network, device, user. The PDS authenticates the request where needed, and admits it with a 2xx response. It then sends a NOTIFY containing either the profile data or content indirection information, which is a pointer for the device to follow.

Content retrieval follows a pointer. Devices and PDSs MUST implement HTTP and HTTPS for this. In change notification, whenever a profile changes the PDS MUST inform every device enrolled for it, using a NOTIFY that carries the changes, a revised profile, or a pointer to the new data. The device MUST act on the change before its effective-by time expires.

If enrollment fails, the device retries with exponential back-off. The RFC's pseudo-code waits 2^i * (64*T1) between attempts and caps i at 8. A cached local-network profile MUST NOT be used unless the device can be sure it is on the same local network.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone asks for a settings sheet. The server either hands it over or says where to pick it up. If the sheet changes later, the server tells the phone. If asking fails, the phone waits longer and longer before trying again.

sections.title: Finding the Server and Forming the Request
sections.content:
The device must build a Subscription URI for each profile. Data it uses can be configured, cached or discovered, and it SHOULD prefer them in that order. For the local-network profile, the device gets the local domain name from DHCPv4 or DHCPv6. The Request-URI has no user part, and its host is _sipuaconfig followed by the domain, for example sip:_sipuaconfig.airport.example.net. If no user address of record is configured, the From field is anonymous@anonymous.invalid.

For the device profile, the user part is a device identifier in UUID URN form, escaped in the URI, and the host is the device provider's domain. The device discovers that domain from the DHCP SIP-server option, the DHCP local domain, or the local network domain prefixed with _sipuaconfig, in that order. For the user profile, the Request-URI and From field are both the user's address of record. All requests carry the same +sip.instance value in Contact, which lets a local network track devices and manage resources such as bandwidth.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone writes its request on an envelope. For the building's sheet it uses a special mailbox name, for its own sheet it uses its serial number, and for the user's sheet it uses the user's own address.

sections.title: The ua-profile Event Package
sections.content:
The new SIP event package is named ua-profile and defines five Event header parameters. profile-type takes device, user or local-network. vendor, model and version MUST be sent in every SUBSCRIBE so that the PDS can tailor profiles, and the vendor SHOULD use its DNS domain name. effective-by appears only in NOTIFY and gives the maximum number of seconds before the device MUST try to apply the profile. A value of 0 means immediately, even if service is interrupted, which lets a PDS fix an emergency or disable a device at once.

Other rules: a separate subscription dialog is used for each profile type. The Accept header must list the profile content types wanted, and message/external-body signals support for content indirection. If no duration is given, 86400 seconds (24 hours) is RECOMMENDED. An Expires value of zero gives a one-time fetch. An unavailable profile type SHOULD get a 404, and an unknown device or user MAY be rejected with 403. A subscriber MUST NOT reject an empty NOTIFY, and an empty NOTIFY does not end the subscription. Forked SUBSCRIBEs are not supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The request has a few labels on it: which sheet you want, who made your phone, and which model. The reply can say how fast the phone must switch to the new settings.

sections.title: Securing Profile Delivery
sections.content:
Profiles can hold sensitive data such as identities and credentials, so the framework requires authentication, integrity and, for sensitive data, confidentiality. Devices and PDSs MUST support digest authentication over TLS, and the device MUST also authenticate the PDS. Without TLS, the device MUST NOT respond to authentication challenges, because that would allow offline dictionary attacks. The RFC notes MD5 was considered reasonable in RFC 3261 and recommends stronger alternatives such as SHA-256.

For content indirection, sensitive profiles MUST use an HTTPS URI, and HTTP MUST NOT carry sensitive data except when bootstrapping through the device profile. Sensitive change notifications SHOULD use the SIP Identity header, and the PDS MUST use content indirection when the contact URI is not SIPS or the enrollment was not authenticated.

Bootstrapping is the hard case: a new or factory-reset device has no credentials. It can be pre-configured, receive credentials out of band, get them from the user, or receive them in the device profile. The last option MUST be supported. Such a device is at the mercy of the network it asks, so credentials handed out this way MUST be quickly replaced by large-entropy ones.
sections.plainLanguage: Settings can include secret passwords, so the phone and server must check each other's identity and talk privately. A brand new phone has no secrets yet, so it needs extra care the first time.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the ua-profile event package and added the five new Event header parameters (profile-type, vendor, model, version and effective-by) to its SIP header parameter registry. Only profile-type has predefined values.

The RFC also creates a new registry of SIP Configuration Profile Types, with registration by Specification Required. A registration must include the profile type and a published document describing its purpose and usage. The initial entries are local-network, device and user.
sections.plainLanguage: The new names were written in an official list so nobody else uses them for something different, and new types of settings sheets can be added to the list later.
